content:
Over the past three studies we have been walking through the burnt offering animals that each tribal leader brought to the altar of dedication the young bull of total strength and surrender, the ram of substitution caught in the thicket, and the one-year-old lamb that was the Passover promise fulfilled. Today we step back and look at all three together, because there is something remarkable in the combination of these three animals that we would miss if we only studied each one on its own. And there is something equally remarkable in the total number of burnt offerings once all twelve leaders had completed their twelve days of offering.

Did you notice that the burnt offering was not one animal? Each leader brought three: a young bull, a ram, and a male lamb of the first year. Three different animals. Three different characters. Three different messages about Christ’s sacrifice. And this combination of three is not accidental. Three in Scripture consistently speaks of completeness across time; the past, the present, and the future. And Peter, in his second letter, gives us the precise framework for understanding the three ages of God’s plan with the world.

In 2 Peter 3:5-7 and 2 Peter 3:13, Peter describes three distinct ages of heaven and earth. The first was the heaven and earth that was; the world from Adam to Noah, the age that ended in the flood when God judged the wickedness of that generation. The second is the heaven and earth that is the present world, the age we are living in now, which Peter says is being kept for fire, reserved for the day of judgment. And the third is the new heaven and new earth that is to come the age described in Revelation 21, the eternal age after the thousand-year Kingdom has been completed, when God makes all things new and dwells with His people forever. Three ages. A beginning age, a present age, and an eternal age. Past, present, and future all within the plan of God.

The three burnt offering animals span these three ages in the sacrifice of Christ. The young bull speaks of the first age the age of Adam, the age of fallen man in his strength and condition, the age that required a servant who would bear the griefs and carry the sorrows of the original broken humanity. The ram speaks of the present age the age of substitution, the age in which the condemned are released because another has taken their place, the age in which the gospel of the cross is preached to every creature. And the one-year-old lamb speaks of the age to come; the firstfruits lamb, the Passover lamb whose blood covers the household for eternity, the Lamb who stands at the centre of the throne in Revelation 5 in the new creation, still bearing the wounds. Three animals.

Three ages. One sacrifice that covers all three.

This is why Paul could write in Hebrews 9:26: “But as it is, He has appeared once for all at the end of the ages (Jewish age) to put away sin by the sacrifice of Himself.” Once for all; not once for the present age only. Not once for the people alive at the time of the cross only. Once for all the ages. The young bull, the ram, and the lamb together were saying: the sacrifice of Christ is not confined to one era of history. It reaches backward to Adam and forward to eternity. The burnt offering of the three animals together is a single act of redemption that covers the whole span of God’s plan beginning, middle, and endless end.

When all twelve tribal leaders had completed their offerings over twelve days, the total number of burnt offering animals was 36. Twelve young bulls, twelve rams, twelve one-year-old lambs; three animals per leader, twelve leaders, making thirty-six animals in all. And the number 36 is not a neutral number in Scripture. It appears in two significant moments, and both times it is connected with the same sobering theme: the breaking of covenant, the shifting of trust away from Yahweh, and the consequence that follows.

The first appearance is in Joshua 7. Israel had just experienced the miraculous fall of Jericho; the walls collapsed, the city was taken, and the name of Yahweh was feared throughout the land. But a man named Achan had secretly taken some of the devoted things that Yahweh had commanded to be set apart.

The covenant had been broken in secret, by one man, hidden from sight.
When Israel then went up against the small town of Ai, expecting an easy victory, they were soundly defeated. Joshua 7:5 records the consequence:
the men of Ai chased the Israelites and killed about thirty-six of them as they retreated. Thirty-six deaths. Thirty-six lives lost because one man had broken the covenant of Yahweh. The number 36 sat over Israel like a mark of judgment the number of the broken covenant and its cost.

Now here is where it becomes deeply meaningful. We have three animals and twelve leaders making thirty-six burnt offerings. And 36 carries the weight of broken covenant, of the gap between a holy God and a disobedient people, of the judgment that follows when the covenant is violated. Christ steps into that number. His thirty-six burnt offering animals; spread over twelve days, brought by twelve leaders are placing the full weight of broken covenant before the altar of Yahweh. And that is exactly what Christ came to do. But before we see how He reverses it, there is a second story connected to 36 that we must look at tomorrow. It is the story of a king who began well and ended badly, and the thirty-sixth year of his reign is one of the most searching warnings in all of Scripture. We will continue tomorrow.

title: Prayer
text:
Great is Yahweh, and greatly to be praised; His greatness is unsearchable (Psalm 145:3). We thank You that the sacrifice of Christ is not limited to one age, one generation, or one era of history. Three animals on the altar; and all three ages of Your plan are covered. The world that was, the world that is, and the world that is to come are all held in the one offering of Your Son. We thank You that He appeared once for all at the end of the ages so that no age would be left uncovered, no generation without a ransom, no era of human history outside the reach of His atonement. As we see the number 36 beginning to speak, prepare our hearts for what it is saying. Help us to hear not only the comfort of the sacrifice but the weight of what was broken that made it necessary.
In Christ’s name, amen.
